u2-l01.title: Castling
u2-l01.summary: King and rook in a single move

u2-l01-s01.text: Castling moves the king and a rook in the same move. The king goes two squares toward the rook, and the rook jumps to the other side of the king. This is kingside castling: O-O.

u2-l01-s02.text: Queenside castling goes toward the rook on a1: the king goes to c1 and the rook to d1. It's written O-O-O.

u2-l01-s03.hint: Tap the king and then g1: the king moves two squares toward the rook.
u2-l01-s03.success: Correct. The king is safe on g1, and the rook moved to f1.

u2-l01-s04.hint: Move the king two squares toward the rook on a8.
u2-l01-s04.success: Correct. The king went to c8 and the rook to d8.

u2-l01-s05.text: To castle, the king and that rook can't have moved at any point in the game, and the squares between them must be empty.

u2-l01-s06.text: You also can't castle if the king is in check, or if it passes through or lands on an attacked square. Here the black bishop attacks f1: no kingside castling, but queenside is fine.

options: No, the king would land on an attacked square
No, the rook is under attack
u2-l01-s07.explanation: The knight attacks g1, the square where the king would land. That's why kingside castling isn't allowed.
feedback: Look at which squares the knight on h3 attacks.
The rook on h1 isn't attacked, and even if it were, that wouldn't stop you from castling.

u2-l01-s08.explanation: Nothing is attacked on the queenside: the king passes through d1 and lands on c1 with no problem.
feedback: Check d1 and c1: neither is attacked.

u2-l02-s01.text: If a pawn advances two squares and lands next to an enemy pawn, the enemy pawn can capture it as if it had advanced only one square. This is called en passant.

u2-l02-s02.text: You can only do it on the very next move. If you play something else, you lose the right.

u2-l02-s03.prompt: Black just played f5. Capture en passant.
u2-l02-s03.hint: The f-pawn advanced two squares and landed next to yours. Capture it by going to f6.
u2-l02-s03.success: Correct. Your pawn is on f6 and the pawn on f5 left the board.

u2-l02-s04.prompt: You're playing Black. White just played b4. Capture en passant.
u2-l02-s04.hint: The b-pawn advanced two squares and landed next to your pawn on c4.
u2-l02-s04.success: Correct. Your pawn is on b3 and the pawn on b4 left the board.

u2-l02-s05.prompt: Black just played d5. Where does your pawn end up if it captures en passant?
u2-l02-s05.explanation: It ends up on d6, the square the black pawn skipped. The pawn on d5 leaves the board.
feedback: You capture as if the pawn had advanced just one square.
The pawn captures diagonally.

u2-l02-s06.prompt: Black played d5 two moves ago. Can you still capture en passant?
u2-l02-s06.explanation: En passant is only allowed on the move right after the two-square advance.
feedback: It's only allowed on the very next move.

u2-l02-s07.prompt: Black just played e5, advancing two squares. Tap the pawn you can capture en passant.
u2-l02-s07.hint: It's the pawn that just advanced two squares.

u2-l03.title: Promoting well
u2-l03.summary: Choose the right piece when you promote

u2-l03-s01.text: Review: when a pawn reaches the last rank, you choose which piece it becomes. The queen is almost always the right choice.

u2-l03-s02.hint: A pawn can also capture diagonally when it promotes. If it advances to d8, the rook captures it.
u2-l03-s02.success: Correct. You captured the rook and promoted at the same time.

u2-l03-s03.text: Watch out for stalemate. If you promote to a queen here, the black king has no squares and isn't in check: that's stalemate and the game ends in a draw.

u2-l03-s04.prompt: Promote without stalemating the black king, and keep enough material to deliver mate.
u2-l03-s04.hint: A queen would stalemate. Try a rook: it leaves the square a6 free.
u2-l03-s04.success: Correct. With a rook, the black king has a6, and after Ka6 comes Ra8 mate.

u2-l03-s05.prompt: Black threatens Qf1 mate. Which piece should you promote to?
u2-l03-s05.explanation: A knight on d8 checks the king and attacks the queen at the same time. With a queen or a rook, Black mates with Qf1.
feedback: With a queen, Black plays Qf1 and it's mate.
With a rook, Black plays Qf1 and it's mate.

u2-l03-s06.prompt: Promote so that Black can't deliver mate.
u2-l03-s06.hint: Promote to a knight: it gives check and attacks the queen.
u2-l03-s06.success: Correct. After the check, the knight captures the queen.

u2-l03-s07.text: Before promoting, check two things: whether a queen would stalemate the enemy king, and whether you can be mated afterward. It's almost always a queen; sometimes, another piece.

u2-l04.title: Stalemate
u2-l04.summary: No moves and no check: a draw

u2-l04-s01.text: Black to move, but the king has no safe square and isn't in check. That's stalemate: the game ends in a draw.

u2-l04-s02.text: Here, on the other hand, the king is in check and can't escape: that's mate. The difference between mate and stalemate is the check.

u2-l04-s03.prompt: Black to move. Mate or stalemate?
u2-l04-s03.explanation: The black king has no squares, but it isn't in check: stalemate, a draw.
feedback: Is the king in check?

u2-l04-s04.prompt: Black to move. Mate or stalemate?
u2-l04-s04.explanation: The queen gives check and the king can't escape or capture it, because the white king protects it: that's mate.
feedback: See if the queen gives check.

u2-l04-s05.prompt: White to move. Which of these moves stalemates the black king?
u2-l04-s05.explanation: After Qg6, the black king has no squares and isn't in check: stalemate. Qh3, on the other hand, is mate.
feedback: Qh3 gives check, so it isn't stalemate. In fact, it's mate.
Qd8 gives check and the king escapes to h7.

u2-l04-s06.hint: Your king already controls g7 and g8. Give check along the h-file.
u2-l04-s06.success: Correct. Qh3 is mate: the black king is in check and has nowhere to go.

u2-l04-s07.text: If you're losing, stalemate can save you. Here Black has a queen, but White has no moves and isn't in check: a draw.

u2-l05-s01.text: Black has more material and threatens mate, but White gives check after check. If the same position occurs three times, the game is a draw.

u2-l05-s02.text: This is called perpetual check: endless checks your opponent can't avoid. It's the most common way to save a lost game by repetition.

u2-l05-s03.prompt: You're losing and Black threatens mate. Give check to start the perpetual.
u2-l05-s03.hint: Look for a queen check where the queen can't be captured.
u2-l05-s03.success: Correct. With endless checks, Black can't avoid the draw.

u2-l05-s04.text: It's also a draw when neither side has enough material to deliver mate: king against king, king and bishop against king, or king and knight against king.

u2-l05-s05.prompt: King and rook against king. Is that enough to deliver mate?
u2-l05-s05.explanation: Yes: king and rook can deliver mate. You'll see how in the endgames unit.
feedback: The rook, with help from the king, can deliver mate.

u2-l05-s06.prompt: King and knight against king. Is that enough to deliver mate?
u2-l05-s06.explanation: No: you can't force mate with a single knight. It's a draw by insufficient material.
feedback: A lone knight isn't enough to deliver mate.

u2-l05-s07.text: The 50-move rule: if each side plays 50 moves with no captures and no pawn moves, it's a draw. Players can also agree to a draw: in Bots you can offer one to your opponent.

u2-l05-s08.prompt: Which of these situations is not a draw?
u2-l05-s08.explanation: Checkmate ends the game with a winner. The other two are draws.
feedback: Stalemate is a draw.
Threefold repetition is a draw.

u2-l06-s01.text: Each move is written with the piece's letter and the square it goes to: K king, Q queen, R rook, B bishop and N knight (K is already taken by the king). This move is Nf3. Pawns have no letter: e4.

u2-l06-s02.text: If the move is a capture, add an x: Bxd5. When a pawn captures, write the file it comes from: exd5.

u2-l06-s03.text: Other symbols: + is check and # is mate, like Qxf7# in this position. O-O is kingside castling, O-O-O is queenside castling, and =Q shows a promotion: e8=Q.

u2-l06-s04.prompt: How do you write the knight's move from g1 to f3?
feedback: K is the king.
B is the bishop.

u2-l06-s05.hint: B is the bishop: move the bishop from f1 to c4.
u2-l06-s05.success: Correct. Bc4: the bishop went to c4.

u2-l06-s06.hint: The pawn on the e-file captures on d5.
u2-l06-s06.success: Correct. exd5: the e-pawn captured on d5.

u2-l06-s07.explanation: O-O-O is queenside castling, toward the rook on the a-file. O-O is kingside castling.
feedback: Kingside castling has two Os: O-O.
Mate is shown with #.

options: A pawn promotes to a knight on e8 and gives check
A knight goes to e8 and gives check
A pawn promotes to a queen on e8
u2-l06-s08.explanation: e8 is the square, =N the piece it promotes to, and + the check.
feedback: If it were a knight, it would start with N: Ne8+.
=N means knight, not queen.

u2-l06-s09.text: Other languages use other letters: in Spanish, for example, the knight is C, so Nf3 is written Cf3. In this app you'll see K, Q, R, B and N in lessons, games, openings and analysis.
